title: Hallucinations in Bibliographic Recommendation: Citation Frequency as a Proxy for Training Data Redundancy
research_target: Test whether citation frequency predicts bibliographic recall fidelity and hallucination
study_setting: 20 CS topics; GPT-4.1 API
data_source: GPT-4.1 outputs; Google Scholar citation counts; Sentence-BERT metadata comparison
sample_size: 100 generated records: 5 papers for each of 20 CS topics
time_window: Generated in 2025; GPT-4.1 knowledge cutoff June 2024; Google Scholar citation counts retrieved October 2025
treatment_or_system_conditions: Single parametric GPT-4.1 condition; JSON output without explanations or IDK response
comparison_or_control: High-citation versus low-citation records split at median citation count; cross-topic comparison
ground_truth_or_labeling: Manual existence and metadata verification in Google Scholar; factual score 0/1/2; cosine similarity between generated and authentic metadata
main_outcomes: Factual score; hallucination rate; metadata cosine similarity; citation count; topic-level variation

key_controls_or_adjustments: Topic diversification across 20 CS domains; citation count treated as proxy for training-data redundancy

key_design_strength: Clear mechanism test linking prior visibility to parametric recall accuracy
key_design_limitation: Small sample; single model; citation count is only a proxy for training exposure; does not measure human citation choice
reusable_element_for_our_study: Use as a parametric-memory baseline; measure whether long-tail papers are less accurately recalled even when relevant
